title: How to Have Fun Helping Your Students Value School This Year
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: This piece opens Stuart's August 2022 series on building student Value, framing the classroom as a "cosmos," an alternate, orderly world students are invited into that inevitably requires discomfort, sacrifice, and work. He catalogs the familiar complaints and groans students produce when they don't yet value an assignment, "This is boring," "Why do we have to do this?", and argues these reactions are a normal feature of classroom life, not evidence of teacher failure. His central move is to reframe the goal: rather than being frightened or defensive when students groan, teachers should become so secure in the goodness of what they're offering that they can respond with genuine enjoyment rather than anxiety. He offers writing class and PE as parallel examples of subjects students often resist initially but come to value once they experience what the discipline actually offers. The piece functions as the introduction and thesis statement for a longer series that Stuart later expanded into standalone posts on the Rainbow of Why, Caroline Ong's example, and Bill Damon's purpose research.
points: Stuart reframes the classroom itself as a "cosmos," an intentionally different world students are invited into, which explains why discomfort is a normal and expected part of learning.
He explicitly treats student groans and resistance, "This is boring," "Whyyyyyyy?!", as unremarkable classroom weather rather than a signal that something has gone wrong.
The core reframe, having fun while stoking Value rather than treating resistance defensively, models an emotional posture, not just a technique.
This post functions as the thesis-setting introduction to a full August 2022 series on building student Value, later split into the Rainbow of Why, Apologist Winsome and Sure, and Bill Damon pieces.
quotes: When students don't optimally Value school, they'll say things like this: This is boring. This is pointless. Why do we have to do this?

Here's why: your classroom is an alternate world from the one your students normally inhabit. Or at least, it should be. It's a cosmos — Latinized from the Greek kosmos: a good order, an orderly arrangement; a world.

Whether you teach art or agriculture, social studies or Scripture, English language arts or personal finance, you are, day by day, through helping your students toward mastery of your discipline, inviting them in to a cosmos.

When your students respond to your high-impact lessons with moans and groans, this need not frighten or bother you. There's a way to become so sure of the goodness of what you have on offer in your cosmos that you don't bat an eye when folks are genuinely hesitant about its goodness.

They don't like writing right now, and you can relate to that: after all, writing is hard and often proves to us how foggy our thinking is. But you can still have fun as the writing teacher because you know they'll come round.
